#80567. Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2039 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

Yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

Back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

According to recent reports, sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

According to recent reports, back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

In a recent development, the same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses organization-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these fresh systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

After all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

According to recent reports, the main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

It has been revealed that one strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more swiftly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

But, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

It has been revealed that also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a latest tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

According to recent reports, that doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

According to recent reports, at a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

They need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

In a recent development, but formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff indicated their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a big downside… mistakes will be made.

Recent findings suggest that many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a latest tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

According to recent reports, I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

What they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

It has been revealed that this time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Sources indicate that look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

Staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

But too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

Recent findings suggest that that said, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

Again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

Today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are currently bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

And that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

Sources indicate that that is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Company data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

The instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it highlights exactly where the official tools are falling short.

Look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

Sources indicate that I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

However, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out new technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.

  • The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.
  • The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.

The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

In a recent development, “By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved. Given so few works of this kind survive intact, its preservation makes it especially valuable,” states a statement from the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The volumes were kept in a private collection from the 1980s until 2020 when they were sold at Sotheby’s London for £620,000 (before fees) to a specialist dealer in London.

The calligraphic works, thought to be over 400 years old, are spread across 29 leaves and feature gold ornamentation of plant and animal motifs. The two volumes derive from an imperial album created around 1595-1605.

Recent findings suggest that according to the DCMS statement, the original album was prepared for Mughal Emperor Akbar or his son Prince Salim at the royal workshop either in Lahore or Agra. Muhammad Hussain Kashmiri and Abd al-Rahim al-Haravi are among the calligraphers featured.

The Black Prince marble bust by Michael Rysbrack (around 1735).

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.

Meanwhile another export bar has been placed on a marble bust of the 14th-century prince Edward of Woodstock, the son of King Edward III of England and popularly known as the Black Prince. Created around 1735, the sculpture was made by the Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack.

This export bar will initially expire on 5 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £496,044 plus VAT, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Fiona Twycross, the heritage minister, claims in a statement: “For nearly three hundred years [the sculpture] has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Maker's Mark brand identity around its red wax, casting Star Hill Farm materials into marks that tell the story.

The bottle does the talking. Turner Duckworth kept the hand-dipped red top exactly where it belongs, at the center of the system, then built a whole language out of it. Wheat stalks, oak rings and native flora from Star Hill Farm were dipped and cast in the same red wax, so the marks that carry the brand are literal pieces of the place. Against a Wheat Cream ground, the red reads as one loud note in a quiet room, with Printmaker's Black holding the type steady.

The type comes from a person, not a library. Co-founder Margie Samuels shaped the original bottle, and the studio recreated her handwriting as a custom typeface with Nick Cooke at G-Type. Hundreds of characters, contextual alternates and ligatures keep it feeling handwritten rather than set, and her voice runs through the labels, menus and posters in a flowing, wax-like hand.

Industry observers note that layouts stay plain on purpose. A letterhead puts the Samuels family's SIV mark at the center and the distillery address in the corner, so place sits at the heart of every sheet. Type stays large and calm, with room around it, and the wordmark does its work without decoration.

In a recent development, the palette is the bottle, remembered in three tones. Wheat Cream is the ground, true to the label. Printmaker's Black carries the type. Wax Red does the rest, in finish and in form: powder-coated metal, glazing and varnish applied to objects with smooth, flowing shapes. The same red runs across mugs, folders, books and table tents, so every object in the world feels dipped from the same pot.

Sources indicate that scott Grummett photographed the world at Star Hill Farm in warm cream tones and natural light, with touches of glossy wax red. The pictures tell the slower story behind the liquid: hand-rotated barrels, hand-cut labels, hand-dipped bottles, and the land that gives it flavour.

#80563. Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

📅 2026-10-20 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

As someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a big part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is at the moment rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

And my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

Industry observers note that because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

According to recent reports, take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

Recent findings suggest that on the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

Randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

Sources indicate that to see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

The random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:.

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:.

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:.

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

In a recent development, the optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:.

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

Normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

That’s where the caching key comes in:.

In the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped).

To see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:.

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e91-4bac-765e-b04e-a53636759163) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:.

Sources indicate that there’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:.

This can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

And now for the practical part.

According to recent reports, when I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

Think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-157f-708d-a704-fa067114aaca) by @utilitybend.

Here is the CSS powering the letters:.

Sources indicate that I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

One quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:.

Screen reader owners get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

According to recent reports, I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-c117-729f-9844-ddf19fc1fc96) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:.

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

If you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

Industry observers note that we’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

Industry observers note that for dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:.

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e93-849d-72a9-9254-3f4305e58a34) by @utilitybend.

Here’s how I put that together:.

In a recent development, in the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

Industry observers note that here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e94-79c6-70b1-97d4-66b7c2d736b0) by @utilitybend.

Look at how cleanly this works:.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:.

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-4cbe-77bd-9128-685d2c75cc56) by @utilitybend.

Sources indicate that calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

Industry observers note that I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:.

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-fe50-76dc-943b-d75fcaf704e6) by @utilitybend.

Recent findings suggest that some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

Recent findings suggest that but! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:.

If someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

Tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

It has been revealed that we spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

#80560. Latest bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1283 w)

Latest bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed?
  • Industry observers note that juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence.
  • Industry observers note that though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura, a fresh bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.

Industry observers note that juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration problems, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020).

Industry observers note that though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.

“On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper. “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.

Central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo says, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”.

Detail of Justin Favela's Mantecore (White Tiger) (2017), featured in Qué tanto es tantito, a group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso.

Sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite, which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, rolled out in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is right now in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.

In a recent development, “A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales says. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”.

The Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” says Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.

Sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.

According to recent reports, “There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” claims Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”.

Installation view of the group show Costuras Territoriales at the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso Courtesy of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso.

According to recent reports, in El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December), curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra says. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”.

Recent findings suggest that independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea, exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo, will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” notes Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation, which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff, a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.

Installation view ofthe group exhibiton Qué tanto es tantito, group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso.

According to recent reports, sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta, presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.

Sources indicate that picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other issues. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he says.

Sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo claims. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”.

  • Sources indicate that so what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that so what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

It has been revealed that well, research demonstrates that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

The findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, users expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a fresh page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

Recent findings suggest that many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

According to recent reports, the rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

Using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a new page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

It’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow owners to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

Sources indicate that for accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

Arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

The safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

It has been revealed that but we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — shows all options and allows users to drill down.

According to recent reports, and if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

According to recent reports, the objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a newly introduced collaboration between ESR, a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl—which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Sources indicate that across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal character.

Sources indicate that behind the playful graphics are the practical features that define ESR’s accessories. The Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand incorporates a built-in adjustable stand, MagSafe compatibility, and protective construction, allowing it to move between different activities without sacrificing its colorful design. Coordinating magnetic wallets hold cards and cash in compact silhouettes, while the Magnetic Wallet Stand with Grip adds an adjustable viewing stand and finger loop for greater versatility. Together, these features bring Craig & Karl’s expressive graphics to everyday accessories.

The collection’s appeal also comes from the way it brings art into objects that have become nearly inseparable from modern life. Where traditional artworks invite observation, these designs encourage interaction, becoming more personal through repeated use. A phone placed on a café table, a wallet retrieved during a morning commute, or a device propped against a desk becomes a small, unexpected moment of visual interest.

With Pocket Full of Joy, ESR and Craig & Karl make a case for bringing more creativity into the everyday. Sometimes, the most memorable design details are found in the things we carry without a second thought.

According to recent reports, the ESR × Craig & Karl Pocket Full of Joy collection will be available Nov. 14, 2026, at esr.com and amazon.com, with iPhone cases starting at $49.99 and magnetic wallets starting at $25.99.

For a newly introduced residence in Orange County, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway approached that challenge through a careful balance of natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings. The goal was to create a home that felt as warm and comfortable as it was refined, with a relaxed atmosphere suited to everyday family life.

Recent findings suggest that galloway drew inspiration from the architecture and natural surroundings, aiming to create a timeless home. The interiors are organized around texture and natural materials in a soft, understated palette. Warm woods, soft neutrals, and natural stone run through the rooms alongside linen, wool, and mohair.

According to recent reports, tactile upholstery and darker accents contrast with the lighter woods and stone, adding depth and dimension to each room. Furniture was selected for comfort and sculptural appeal, with clean lines and soft, organic forms, giving rooms a relaxed, lived-in quality.

The attention to detail extends to the home’s fixtures and finishes. Hardware from Rocky Mountain Hardware and Nanz is complemented by mirrors from Claude Home and Croft House, while lighting comes from Ravenhill, Atelier de Troupe, and Roll & Hill.

The kitchen, primary bathroom, and living room carry the same combination of wood, stone, and natural fibers. Beyond the main rooms, the property includes a separate guest house with its own bedroom and an indoor-outdoor living area. Galloway extended the same material palette to these spaces, creating continuity throughout the property.

Rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Galloway lets the interplay of materials, textures, and forms define the interiors. It’s an approach that brings warmth and intimacy to a home of considerable scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.

Sources indicate that the gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL. Anyone who has eaten under those Guastavino vaults knows the sign on the wall. Rudolph de Harak packed its letters tight, rimmed them in heavy black outlines, and filled them with colors straight out of a crayon box. Against wood paneling and old tile, it has always looked like the one guest in the room who came to have fun. Pentagram started from a simple question: what would the rest of that alphabet look like?

In a recent development, the answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals. Strokes run broad, corners clip short, and counters turn angular. The O is an octagon with a diamond punched through its middle, and that shape sets the rules for every other character. Blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple take turns filling the forms.

Storefront Gala 2026 appears in compact stacks and stepped arrangements, with rotated numerals adding an unexpected twist. Letters meet along their black outlines and lock into continuous compositions that feel assembled from colorful building blocks. A smaller sans serif organizes the event information around these expressive forms, holding the honorees, the venue, and the date in quiet lines above the noise.

Recent findings suggest that the system runs across digital announcements, posters, a folded program, screen graphics, and embroidered caps. Some pieces set the colored letters on white, while others flood the ground with a single saturated color and let the type push back. The folded program carries the full stack in a run of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple, with the small sans serif keeping the facts straight at the top of the sheet.

In a recent development, the caps are the most tactile piece of the set, the lettering stitched small across white, green, and pale blue cotton. An orange sign stands on the tiled floor, and the word SALOON stretches across a wood doorway in the same blocky letters, proof the alphabet holds its shape from a poster down to a doorway. Pentagram has designed identities for Storefront since 2012, and this one plays the longest with the room it was made for.

Nan Goldin to debut upcoming film exploring nature and extinction in first UK solo museum show in over two decades

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise.
  • What links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation?
  • Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.

What links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

According to recent reports, rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents new and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.

Sources indicate that the show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a new score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part I, 2024.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Recent findings suggest that it accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.

Elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.

Art of intimacy: Young Love (2024) is one of Goldin’s works in Stendhal Syndrome © Nan Goldin; courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Industry observers note that for Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas states. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”.

• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-14 March 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it. But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

According to recent reports, for this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with new technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store.

The boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. Studebaker’s retro-inspired design brings the 1980s into the present with Bluetooth connectivity, a CD player, USB playback, and a cassette deck that can even record music. A rechargeable battery and built-in carrying handle make it easy to take the nostalgia wherever the party goes.

The SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox is available at store.moma.org for $250.

Photography courtesy of Polaroid.

It has been revealed that polaroid’s Mod puts creative controls directly on the camera, inviting experimentation without the distraction of a smartphone screen. Dedicated physical controls make it easy to explore effects like double exposures, light painting, motion freeze, and split-shot compositions. It’s a refreshingly hands-on approach to photography that encourages a little spontaneity and plenty of happy accidents.

The Polaroid Mod Instant Camera is available at polaroid.com for $169.99.

Photography courtesy of Therabody.

Therabody takes a different approach to workout recovery with a device designed to fit between your hands. To help manage body heat during workouts, the handheld device uses temperature-controlled surfaces to cool both palms simultaneously, with additional heat and contrast therapy settings. Compact and cordless, it provides an alternative to ice baths and other more cumbersome temperature-based recovery equipment.

The CryoTherm Palm is available at therabody.com for $399.99.

Photography courtesy of Balmuda.

Inspired by traditional pocket watches, Balmuda’s The Clock reimagines how we experience time through light, sound, and movement. Its carved aluminum body houses 75 LEDs that create an animated display, while built-in speakers play ambient soundscapes designed for focus, relaxation, and sleep. With customizable alarms, app connectivity, and USB-C charging, it’s a thoughtful alternative to the conventional bedside clock.

The Clock is available at us.balmuda.com for $499 in Silver and $519 in Champagne.

Photography courtesy of Bang & Olufsen.

Industry observers note that bang & Olufsen’s Beoplay H100 headphones are undeniably a splurge, but they’re designed with longevity in mind. The Danish brand developed the H100 with replaceable components, including the ear cushions, headband, and batteries. The custom titanium drivers, soft leather detailing, and rich color options give them a distinctly luxurious feel, while advanced noise cancellation and immersive sound make the listening experience just as considered as the design. It’s an investment piece for someone who appreciates exceptional craftsmanship as much as great audio.

The Beoplay H100 Headphones are available at bang-olufsen.com for $2,200.

Photography courtesy of Warby Parker.

Industry observers note that smart glasses are getting a stylish upgrade thanks to Warby Parker’s collaboration with Google and Samsung. Available in three of the brand’s familiar silhouettes, the lightweight frames incorporate a camera, open-ear speakers, and Gemini AI for hands-free photography, calls, navigation, and more. Subtly translucent temples offer a glimpse of the technology inside without compromising the classic eyewear design. With prescription, nonprescription, reading, and sunglass options, they’re a surprisingly versatile gift.

Intelligent Eyewear is available for preorder at warbyparker.com, starting at $395.

Photography courtesy of Flowtica.

What looks like an ordinary ballpoint pen has a few technological tricks up its sleeve. The Flowtica Scribe combines a functional writing instrument with an AI-powered voice recorder, allowing owners to capture conversations while taking notes on paper the old-fashioned way. A companion app can transcribe recordings and turn them into summaries and action items, bringing digital convenience to a familiar analog tool. An optional vegan leather charging case gives the device a place to rest between meetings.

The Flowtica Scribe is available at flowtica.ai for $159.

Photography courtesy of Bellroy.

Anyone who’s ever untangled a mess of charging cables at the bottom of a bag will appreciate Bellroy’s thoughtfully designed Tech Kit. The small organizer opens flat to reveal a series of mesh pockets and elastic loops that keep chargers, cables, earbuds, and other tech essentials neatly in place. Its structured shape makes everything easy to see and access, while the streamlined exterior, made from recycled woven fabric, slips neatly into a backpack or carry-on. It’s a simple solution to one of travel’s most persistent little annoyances.

The Tech Kit is available at bellroy.com for $59–$69, depending on color.

Amazon’s latest Kindle redesign brings a more refined look and feel to the familiar e-reader. The Paperwhite Signature Edition pairs a sleek aluminum body with a 7-inch, glare-free display, adjustable warm lighting, and double-tap page turning. Waterproof construction and wireless charging make it an easy travel companion, while two finishes, Graphite and Seaglass Green, offer a choice between classic and colorful.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is available at amazon.com for $250.

Photography courtesy of Daily Objects.

Who says charging stations have to be boring? DailyObjects’ Surge Foldaway turns an everyday tech essential into a sculptural desktop accessory. Its adjustable design accommodates an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods simultaneously, consolidating three charging spots into one tidy footprint. The bold Cosmic Orange finish adds a welcome pop of color, giving the accessory a presence even when the devices are elsewhere.

The Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger is available at dailyobjects.us for $175.

Photography courtesy of ModRetro.

Recent findings suggest that A love letter to handheld gaming, ModRetro’s Chromatic brings the original Game Boy experience into the present with a few thoughtful upgrades. Its magnesium-alloy body houses a custom, pixel-perfect display designed to play original Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges. The colorful finishes include four translucent options that expose the internal hardware, turning the console’s components into part of its visual identity.

The Chromatic + Tetris Bundle is available at modretro.com starting at $199.

Shark’s CryoGlow Plus combines two skincare technologies in a single wearable device: LED light therapy and under-eye cooling. Red, blue, and infrared lights power several treatment modes, while adjustable cooling pads help refresh tired eyes. The upgraded design offers improved LED coverage around the eyes and mouth, and the soft Pastel Berry finish makes this wearable gadget surprisingly stylish.

The CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask is available at sharkninja.com for $379.99.

In a recent development, in a market crowded with phones competing for attention, the Mudita Kompakt is designed to demand less of it. Its minimalist design centers on a 4.3-inch E Ink display, favoring a restrained interface over colorful notifications and app-heavy screens. Essential features like calling, messaging, offline maps, and a camera remain, while a dedicated offline switch offers a physical way to disconnect.

The Mudita Kompakt is available at mudita.com for $399.

Recent findings suggest that who says smart technology has to look high-tech? Birdfy’s Feeder Wood combines the charm of a traditional wooden birdhouse with a built-in camera, letting bird lovers watch their feathered visitors up close. Made from FSC-certified wood, the solar-powered feeder captures 1080p video. Its companion app can identify more than 6,000 bird species, bringing a layer of digital discovery to an otherwise familiar backyard ritual.

The Feeder Wood is available at birdfy.com for $189.99.

Industry observers note that wallie’s approach to the digital photo frame starts with a simple idea: make the screen look less like a screen. Its 10-inch color E Ink display gives photographs the appearance of printed images, while real wood construction and a choice of four finishes help it blend into a gallery wall or shelf arrangement. Rounded or square corners offer further customization, and a rechargeable battery eliminates the need for a visible power cord. Photos can be updated remotely through an app.

The Wallie 10 is available at shop.wallieframe.com for $299.

According to recent reports, with its simple spherical form, Eve Flare looks more like an illuminated object than a conventional lamp. The rechargeable, water-resistant light offers millions of customizable colors, with app and voice controls for setting the mood indoors or outside. Its wireless charging base and portable design mean it can move effortlessly from a bedside table to the patio, adding a little atmosphere wherever it lands.

The Eve Flare Portable Smart LED Lamp is available at apple.com for $99.95.

Photography courtesy of Best Buy.

8BitDo borrows the visual language of the original Nintendo Entertainment System for a mechanical keyboard that feels straight out of the 1980s. Chunky gray keys, red accents, and tactile mechanical switches establish the retro aesthetic, while an included joystick and two oversized programmable buttons bring arcade-style controls to the desktop. Bluetooth and wireless connectivity keep the throwback design compatible with contemporary setups.

The 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition is available at bestbuy.com for $79.99.

Photography courtesy of Orbitkey.

Even the most organized desk tends to accumulate charging cables, adapters, and other small tech accessories. Orbitkey’s Nest v2 gives them a designated home in a compact storage box with adjustable dividers and a fabric-lined interior. The removable leather-covered lid doubles as a valet tray and 15W wireless charger, keeping everyday essentials within reach while concealing the clutter underneath.

The Nest v2 is available at orbitkey.com for $125.

Breaking: OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made?
  • Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.
  • “Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the newly introduced Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

Sources indicate that the architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” says Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Industry observers note that reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

It has been revealed that in the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

In a recent development, the store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into newly introduced objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

In a recent development, designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

In a recent development, “We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving new value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

Sources indicate that at the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

In a recent development, murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.
