💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we debuted The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • In a recent development, what I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we debuted The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

In a recent development, what I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

According to recent reports, when I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out plan. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

We spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

According to recent reports, one of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

Industry observers note that in my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

Industry observers note that confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

I’m a major believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

According to recent reports, clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

It got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to plan? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

According to recent reports, this sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

According to recent reports, kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

It has been revealed that my mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

According to recent reports, my conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

According to recent reports, we talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

Listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

Sources indicate that in my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

It has been revealed that we’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

If you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, new perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

Recent findings suggest that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

Industry observers note that all six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Major Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In a recent development, A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

It has been revealed that rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

In a recent development, every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

Recent findings suggest that an AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

We can call that the break-even line. Returns to owners come in three forms:.

Industry observers note that for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool shows the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

Industry observers note that four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

These questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the glitch alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

Sources indicate that count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom claims to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

You can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

Who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

It has been revealed that A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

In a recent development, compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

Industry observers note that for example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

The nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

Sources indicate that every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

Error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

Automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, people stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

Industry observers note that map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

According to recent reports, show users where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

Letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

Still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

Industry observers note that research in radiology indicates how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result revealed how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

It has been revealed that ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

It has been revealed that table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

Put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

Let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

Question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

Question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

It has been revealed that question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

On Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

It has been revealed that question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

Sources indicate that A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

The feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

Two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

Recent findings suggest that everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that upcoming capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

In a recent development, audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

According to recent reports, start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that consumers might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

The attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a upcoming group exhibition.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

According to recent reports, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

The results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

Industry observers note that candelabra by Fort Standard, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

Participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Organization, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

According to recent reports, candelabra by Hanna Anonen, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

Click through the gallery above for a closer look at works featured in the exhibition.

According to recent reports, the exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

It has been revealed that timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

Candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, Newly introduced York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees). That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).

According to recent reports, robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, mentioned in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”.

Sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.

It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.

Claude Monet's La Maison dans les roses.

Sources indicate that on the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.

The piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s New York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.

The evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.

Helen Frankenthaler's Seabreeze.

The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.

Recent findings suggest that rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.

In a recent development, helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.

According to recent reports, the night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas.

David Hockney's David, Celia, Stephen, Ian, London August 1982 (Four Friends) (1982).

And while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.

Nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack.
  • Of course, presentation matters, too.
  • In a recent development, italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

Of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

In a recent development, italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

According to recent reports, from Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Photography courtesy of Artisan Books.

From cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Recent findings suggest that porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing.

Recent findings suggest that long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Published in association with the Smithsonian Institution, it’s a beautiful intersection of art, science, and nature that deserves a place on the coffee table.

Wild Flowers of North America is available at mcgeeandco.com for $72.

According to recent reports, still shopping? Explore Design Milk’s Complete 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for more thoughtful finds for everyone on your list.

Photography courtesy of Maison Plage.

For 100 years, Cahiers d’Art has helped shape the conversation around modern art, championing artists and ideas that challenged convention. Published to celebrate the centennial of the influential Parisian art journal, gallery, and publishing house, A Century of Modernism traces its extraordinary history through archival material, artwork, and contributions from figures including Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, and Marcel Duchamp. With approximately 200 illustrations and a striking graphic cover, the book traces the connections between art, design, and publishing.

Cahiers d’Art: A Century of Modernism is available at maisonplage.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Rizzoli.

In a recent development, for a century, The New Yorker has turned its covers into miniature works of art, capturing everything from everyday New York life to defining cultural moments. Edited by longtime art editor Françoise Mouly, with an introduction by editor-in-chief David Remnick, The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover celebrates that visual legacy through hundreds of illustrations by artists including Saul Steinberg, Roz Chast, Chris Ware, and David Hockney. Spanning 100 years of creativity, the 336-page collection reveals how illustration has shaped the magazine’s distinctive visual identity.

The Newly introduced Yorker: From Cover to Cover is available at barnesandnoble.com for $75.

Photography courtesy of Thames & Hudson.

It has been revealed that food, art, and cultural heritage come together in The Art of Korean Cooking, a visually rich exploration of Korea’s culinary traditions. Created by Onjium, a Seoul-based cultural research institute and Michelin-starred restaurant, the book pairs more than 80 recipes with essays exploring the history, ingredients, and techniques behind Korean cuisine. Beautifully composed photography captures everything from seasonal ingredients to finished dishes, revealing the artistry behind each preparation. With 200 illustrations, the 256-page hardcover is as much a celebration of Korean culture and craftsmanship as it is a cookbook.

The Art of Korean Cooking is available at thamesandhudson.com for $47.

Photography courtesy of teNeues.

In a recent development, not all coffee table books must be about art, architecture, or interiors. Football: The Ultimate Book celebrates America’s favorite sport through striking photography and stories spanning legendary players, iconic stadiums, historic games, and unforgettable Super Bowl moments. This special edition features a handsome black leather-bound cover that gives the 224-page book a sophisticated presence on any coffee table. It’s a winning gift for football fans who appreciate good design.

Football: The Ultimate Book is available at crateandbarrel.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Industry observers note that from Fred Astaire’s effortless elegance to the exuberance of 1960s dance floors, LIFE. Let’s Dance captures the joy of movement through the lens of Life magazine’s legendary photographers. Published by Taschen, the collection brings together more than 200 archival images, many previously unseen, documenting everything from ballet and ballroom to flamenco and the twist. Spanning the late 1930s through the early 1970s, the photographs are accompanied by original magazine covers and commentary from dance critic Lyndsey Winship, offering a lively look at how dance reflects culture, community, and self-expression.

It has been revealed that LIFE. Let’s Dance is available at taschen.com for $50.

Photography courtesy of Wynwood Walls.

From the streets of Paris to collaborations with Chanel and Louis Vuitton, André Saraiva has built a career around his playful, instantly recognizable graffiti character, Mr. A. Published by Rizzoli, Graffiti Life explores the artist’s creative world through painting, photography, graphic design, fashion, and more. The 320-page hardcover is as expressive as its subject, featuring a vibrant cloth cover with foil lettering and seven pop-ups designed by Saraiva himself. It’s a colorful, interactive celebration of an artist who has never been one to stay within the lines.

André Saraiva: Graffiti Life is available at shop.thewynwoodwalls.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Printworks.

The most meaningful coffee table book might be the one you fill yourself. Designed to look like a traditional art book, Printworks’ Life Photo Book features a minimalist beige cloth cover with understated white typography. Inside, 40 sheets of high-quality photo paper offer space to preserve favorite memories, from everyday moments to once-in-a-lifetime adventures. Its expandable binding accommodates photographs as they’re added, transforming a beautifully designed object into a personal keepsake.

The Life Photo Book is available at printworksmarket.com for $39.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Sources indicate that what does contemporary product design look like around the world? Phaidon’s Designed for Life offers a fascinating look at 100 designers pushing the boundaries of furniture, lighting, everyday objects, and more. From established names like Faye Toogood and Sabine Marcelis to emerging talents, the 304-page hardcover explores the materials, techniques, and ideas shaping design today. With 500 illustrations, it’s an inspiring addition to any design enthusiast’s coffee table.

Designed for Life: The World’s Best Product Designers is available at store.hermanmiller.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto has spent his career challenging the boundaries between architecture and nature, creating structures that blur the lines between indoors and out. Published by Taschen, Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today explores three decades of his experimental approach through projects including London’s Serpentine Gallery Pavilion, L’Arbre Blanc in Montpellier, and the Grand Ring at Expo 2025 Osaka. Filled with architectural photography, drawings, and sketches, the oversized, 464-page volume documents the evolution of one of contemporary architecture’s most inventive minds.

Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today is available for preorder at taschen.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

It has been revealed that few people have shaped fashion imagery quite like Grace Coddington. In Grace: The American Vogue Years, the legendary creative director revisits some of her most memorable editorials from 2002 to 2016, including collaborations with photographers Annie Leibovitz, Steven Meisel, and Tim Walker. More than 350 photographs showcase Coddington’s imaginative approach to fashion storytelling, while her behind-the-scenes commentary reveals how the elaborate shoots came together. This updated edition offers a fascinating look at the creative vision behind some of Vogue’s most iconic images.

Grace: The American Vogue Years is available at phaidon.com for $60.

Photography courtesy of Crate & Barrel.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

From maximalist spaces bursting with color to minimalist interiors that celebrate simplicity, Defining Style explores the many ways we make a space our own. Written by Joan Barzilay Freund, the book examines 25 distinct design styles through 150 residential interiors by designers, including spaces by Studio Shamshiri, Laura Gonzalez, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, as well as artist Móyòsóré Martins’ studio. With 260 illustrations and a vibrant, geometric cover, it’s as visually engaging on the coffee table as the spaces featured inside.

Defining Style: The Book of Interior Design is available at phaidon.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Recent findings suggest that art history gets a playful makeover in Assouline’s Art Game Book, which brings an interactive twist to the traditional coffee table book. Through quizzes, puzzles, games, and essays, author David Rosenberg takes readers from Cubism and Dada to Pop Art and contemporary digital art, featuring icons like Warhol, Basquiat, and Dalí along the way. Newly updated for 2026, the oversized, canvas-bound hardcover makes learning about art feel more like play than homework.

The Art Game Book is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

It has been revealed that color takes center stage in Rainbow Dreams, a vibrant exploration of how contemporary artists use the full spectrum to transform their work. Featuring more than 200 artworks by over 100 artists, including Yayoi Kusama, Takashi Murakami, Olafur Eliasson, and Ugo Rondinone, the book spans painting, sculpture, photography, and immersive installations. The 256-page hardcover is a colorful design object in its own right, with a seamless rainbow gradient wrapping around the cover and edges. It’s a joyful addition to any art lover’s collection.

Rainbow Dreams: Color and Light in Contemporary Art is available at phaidon.com for $40.

#80530. Industry News: AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📅 2026-11-17 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1098 w)

Industry News: AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📅 2026-11-17 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Sources indicate that lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

Industry observers note that we asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most noted they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

According to recent reports, these results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

According to recent reports, accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

This matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

Industry observers note that so how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Sources indicate that here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge shows up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only reveals correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

According to recent reports, and it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize concerns. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

Sources indicate that in other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Recent findings suggest that not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

Pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

How many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

According to recent reports, as AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding concerns, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing new gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

According to recent reports, found the issue? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When issues end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

Every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the issue comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

A passing test indicates a known concern hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

Sources indicate that AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

We’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

Sources indicate that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Industry observers note that thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

According to recent reports, it wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

It has been revealed that the evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in May 1986 for $1m.

Gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s New York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Sources indicate that impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s New York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

It has been revealed that french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Substantial name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s New York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

Picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

According to recent reports, the Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s New York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in Upcoming York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

Industry observers note that one of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, Upcoming Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article noted the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

It hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s New York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export concerns, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

According to recent reports, “It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” stated Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

Most of us are still figuring it out and trying to work smarter in this latest world, so we invited industry experts who have been doing this for a while. They show their experience and tell you what works and what doesn’t, so you don’t have to figure it all out yourself.

If you’re interested in AI-ready design systems, AI and Figma, harness engineering, agentic AI UX patterns, and AI workflows for design and engineering teams, this conference is right up your alley!

Showing, not telling: All sessions will be highly practical, focusing on how to integrate AI in your daily work and what to expect in 2027.

We’ll cover the patterns taking shape heading into 2027, from multi-modal experiences to accessibility, and what tends to go wrong along the way. Anna will also show how to add that little bit of delight to your app, and how it can respond to different types of input, whatever the person on the other side of the screen gives you: text, voice or images.

Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” claims Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the fresh attribution.
  • The framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, New York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.

“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” claims Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the fresh attribution.

The framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

Llanes Serrano notes the road to the new attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.

Industry observers note that the early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano claims that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.

Julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s fresh chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day claims.

Llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s fresh conservation studio, says XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the frame of the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

The process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the new 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she claims. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.

A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.

Day claims this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

#80520. Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1901 w)
